summary: Ottawa declares Stellantis in default over the Brampton plant sale and gives it 30 days, as a Microsoft outage disrupts Canadian offices and Carney heads to Manila.
body: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to Stellantis Canada on Thursday to end talks with the carmaker and declare it in default of its 2022 federal funding deal, which promised up to $529 million for its Brampton and Windsor plants.[^1] The trigger is Stellantis's plan to sell its idle Brampton plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel. The company has 30 days to fix the problem, or Ottawa may cancel the agreement and try to recover the money; Joly says the government intends to sue for "hundreds of millions of dollars."[^1][^2] Stellantis has offered to repay at least $220 million voluntarily.[^1]

About 1,800 Brampton workers are still on layoff, getting 70% of their pay plus benefits.[^1] After a Toronto meeting with Stellantis, Unifor and the federal government, Premier Doug Ford said the next step is talks with Stellantis's global CEO, and Joly said both governments will meet him.[^2] Unifor president Lana Payne called the sale "very unfortunate," and the union may seek severance in its contract talks; she says a strike would be a last resort.[^2] Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa had been told of "some aspects" of the deal before it was announced; Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wants Joly removed.[^1]

Elsewhere: a Microsoft outage disrupted email and Teams for governments and businesses across Canada on Thursday and could run into a second day; Microsoft says there is no sign of an attack.[^3] Carney travels on to the ASEAN summit in Manila; Ottawa says it has not abandoned the Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, ahead of a world court ruling due this month on whether Myanmar committed genocide.[^3]
differences: Carney says the government knew of some aspects of the sale in advance; Joly's office says she had no part in negotiating it.[^1] Poilievre says this justifies removing her.[^1]
